subject: dragonling
pitch: A baby dragon the size of a house cat, sitting proudly beside the broken shell of its speckled egg. Teal scales fading to a buttery belly, stubby horns, a row of soft orange spines down its back, oversized wings it can't fly with yet, with translucent amber skin between the fingers, and a chubby tail ending in a little spade. Big amber eyes, a toothy grin and a wisp of smoke curling from one nostril.
reasoning:
I'm sketching out the design for a sitting baby dragon figure, planning proportions roughly cat-sized with an egg shell placed beside it, and working out the skeleton hierarchy starting from the hips to build a natural sitting pose.

Mapping the joint chain from hips through spine, neck, and head using curved paths with specific coordinates and parent-child relationships to shape the dragon's posture.

I'm figuring out the head joint orientation and adding a jaw joint positioned relative to the head using local offsets, then considering how to sweep the body geometry along the spine and neck chain with radius tapering.

Shaping the body radius profile from hips to belly to chest, applying a countershaded scale paint with a lighter belly tone, and sweeping the neck separately with its own tapering radius before building the head from a skull sphere and snout shape.

Still defining jaw geometry...

Explicit bone overrides work fine for the spikes. For the grin I'll pose the jaw bone with a slight forward tilt so the mouth looks toothy and open, applying the pose last so earlier-built pieces follow along. For nostrils I'm thinking small dark spheres at the snout tip, with rising smoke built as a catmull sweep curve that tapers in radius, using light grey since true translucency isn't available.

Positioning eyes as large amber spheres on the head sides, with smaller black pupil spheres offset forward and outward plus a tiny white highlight sphere -- working out the local coordinates for eye and pupil placement relative to the head.

Adding a highlight sphere offset up on the pupil. For the skull, I'm sizing it as an ellipsoid scaled wider than deep so the eyes (radius 0.022) poke out slightly for a cute look, using world-axis scale since there's no explicit orientation. Now I'm adding small brow ridge spheres and starting on cheek details.

Designing horn geometry...

For the dorsal spines, I'm thinking about sweeping small spikes along the spine chain so each one faces outward along the tangent direction, giving a row of ridged bumps down the back.

I'm planning to apply this same spine-sweep technique to the neck and tail, sizing each spike based on its position along the path so the ridge tapers naturally. Now I'm working out the tail shape for a sitting pose, curling it from the hips around toward the front of the body on the ground.

Still plotting tail curve points...

Deciding to orient the spade vertically rather than flat so it reads clearly against the ground, and sketching the outline points for a diamond/lobed spade shape extending along the tail direction with the up axis defined.

Working out the spade orientation geometry...

I'll position it flat at the tail tip, attaching to the last tail joint, colored amber-orange to match the spine color scheme but slightly darker.

Now I'm working out the leg poses for a sitting stance: hind legs with big haunch thighs bent at the knee with feet planted forward, and front legs straight down resting on the ground near the chest, computing hip-to-foot distances and bend directions for each joint using the limb() function.

Still building the foot geometry...

I'm naming the leg joints hip/knee/ankle per side for the rigger, then adding a haunch bulge sphere at the hip bone and starting to position the front arm shoulder and hand targets.

For the arms sitting upright with a slight forward bend, I'm computing shoulder-to-hand distances to check reach against the joint lengths, naming the chain shoulder/elbow/wrist, and parenting it to the spine's third joint near the chest.

Hands get three forward fingers with claw tips like the feet, so I'm placing the wrist and hand joints and double-checking their radii don't dip below ground level. For the wings, since they're oversized and the creature can't fly yet, I'm thinking through a rest pose with arms extending back-up-and-out from the shoulder, three fanning fingers, and an amber translucent membrane, though material limitations mean I can't easily express transparency with a single color.

Since real opacity risks breaking the material baking/atlas process, I'll fake the translucent amber look with a gradient paint instead — darker near the bones, lighter toward the membrane center — and start laying out the wing joint chain from the shoulder root.

I'm plotting the shoulder-elbow-wrist chain and the four finger endpoints that fan outward and curve back to attach the trailing membrane to the body flank, sizing everything oversized relative to the baby dragon's frame so the wings read as large but foldable, partially open rather than overhead.

Now I'm setting up the finger chains themselves, building each as a short polyline from wrist through a midpoint to tip, parented to the arm chain's tip joint so they inherit the wing's pose.

For membranes, I'm connecting adjacent finger chains edge-to-edge to form the webbing, and then figuring out how to close the trailing membrane between the last finger and the body-side line running from wrist back toward the flank.

I'm also considering whether the propatagium between the arm and the leading-edge finger needs its own membrane, but I'll leave that area simple for now and skip adding it.

For membrane edges without an explicit bone, I'm setting them to inherit from the parent spine joint so the blend stays smooth between chains, and setting up a gradient color function that mixes amber tones across the membrane surface.

I'll go with simple amber color strings instead of a mix function since blending might not apply cleanly to colors, picking a few warm shades to alternate across panels for subtle variation, and setting thickness and radii for the wing bones and finger sweeps with a small cream-colored claw spike at the wrist.

Checking wing root placement against the body geometry, the position at x=.055 falls within the spine radius so it's anchored correctly, and the wingspan reaching tip x=.52 looks proportional. Now I'm working out the broken eggshell beside the dragon—sizing it larger than a typical egg since this is a house-cat-sized hatchling, and planning the shell as a lathe-profile lower half with a jagged broken top edge.

Defining the lathe profile outline...

Also thinking about which bone the egg shell should attach to, since it has no joints of its own but should rigidly follow the nearest one, likely the hips or root.

I'll bind the egg explicitly to the hips bone so it moves naturally with the body. Then I'm adding broken shell debris near the egg—a few thin, jagged flat shards lying on the ground with slight thickness, plus a ring of rim shards arranged around the egg's top edge using the ring helper.

Placing small triangular cone shards around that rim, with randomized heights and rotations for an irregular broken-shell look...

I'm deciding to skip the ring-based bone attachment approach and just loop through positions directly in JS, since explicit bone assignment gets messy with that callback system. For the egg surface, I'm adding speckled paint spots in a muted brown over the cream base, possibly varying the coloring between inner and outer shell surfaces.

Now I'm settling on a color palette for the dragon: buttery belly tones, teal body with a darker teal shade, orange spines, cream horns, and amber eyes with dark pupils. I'm considering adding belly striping via a paint function to create subtle countershading rather than a flat color.

I'm applying that same countershaded coat across the body, neck, tail, legs, and head, keeping the lower jaw as plain belly color for contrast, and adding tiny flattened pink-orange discs on the cheeks for a blush effect to make the dragon look cuter.

For proportions I'm thinking cat-sized overall, roughly 0.4 units tall with an oversized head for a baby-dragon look, and I'm working out the body radius taper along the spine chain so the belly looks chubby in the middle while the hips sit low enough to rest naturally on the ground when seated.

Since the cap is a sphere of radius r, the lowest point sits exactly at y=0, which confirms the hip geometry. I'm adjusting the spine points to start at y=0.085 with the hip joint at that same height, working through where the belly center should land around y=0.14.

Checking the tail joints now—each segment's radius needs to match its y-position so the bottom of each circle sits just above or at the floor, tuning points p1 through p4 so they taper smoothly without clipping through the ground. Then I'm setting up the neck chain to connect smoothly from the end of the spine.

Working through the neck-to-head proportions, I realize the dragon's overall height with horns is coming out too tall compared to a house-cat-sized creature, so I'm compressing the neck points to bring the total height down while still keeping a natural curve into the head joint.

Now I'm placing the skull center forward and slightly up from the neck joint, then working out the snout dimensions and jaw box proportions relative to the head's local orientation.

I'm sizing the mouth gap between upper and lower snout surfaces so a 12-degree jaw opening looks right, then positioning upper and lower teeth to span that gap with appropriate lengths and orienting the lower jaw frustum's width and reach along the head's forward axis.

Now I'm placing the jaw's pivot joint near the head base and setting the aim point toward the snout tip, rounding the chin for a softer look, then spacing teeth along the snout at a few forward positions with slight left-right offsets to match the narrowing snout width. For the nostrils, I'm placing small dark spheres near the snout tip and setting up smoke to emit from the left nostril.

Writing smoke curl path...

Checking placement of hind feet against the front hands and belly to avoid limb overlap — nudging hind foot x position outward slightly to keep clearance.

I'm checking the thigh bend distance from hip to ankle, confirming it's within the limb's reach limit so the knee bends naturally outward and upward, and considering how to pass bend directions to the limb function (single direction for all joints vs. per-joint arrays).

I'm placing the thigh blob sphere near the hip joint, scaled and positioned to overlap the body naturally, then working out naming conventions for the front limb joint chains — separating arm joints (shoulder, elbow, hand) from wing joints to avoid naming collisions.

I'm now checking how limb points feed into the chain function, making sure hip-rooted polylines parent correctly on the left/right side, and setting taper radii for hind legs versus front limbs to sweep the geometry along each chain.

I'm working out the shoulder-to-hand geometry, computing distances and bend lengths so the arm chain stays nearly straight with just a slight elbow bend backward, then sketching a toe-adding function that spaces three toes outward from each ankle position.

Now I'm shaping each toe with a tapered capsule in teal and adding a small claw spike pointing outward from the tip, before turning to the wing placement loop that mirrors coordinates across left and right sides relative to the spine.

Working out the remaining finger tip coordinates and the droopy wing membrane path, I'm placing a flank anchor point on the body surface to connect the membrane between the third finger and the torso.

I also need a wrist claw spike at the wing joint, and I'm setting up tapered sweep radii along the arm and finger bone chains so the membrane edges blend smoothly where they share a starting point at the wrist.

Now I'm adding a spine generator that places cone-shaped spikes along the body, varying their size with a sine-based scale factor so they bulge and taper naturally along the spine's length.

Then I extend this to the neck with smaller spines and the tail with its own tapering scale, making sure the spikes always point dorsally even as the tail curls. I'm also setting the spine color to a soft orange tone, then moving on to handle body stripe painting with configurable size, axis, and width options.

Now I'm defining the skeleton joints: hips as a root with the spine chain starting there, then the head jointed off the neck with a jaw that aims forward and down from it, followed by eye and pupil placement.

I'm working out the eye geometry—amber sphere eyes sized to protrude slightly from the skull for a cartoon look, with small white highlight spheres and darker pupils positioned relative to the eye center using offsets for forward, up, and side placement.

Positioning the egg off to the model's right, slightly forward, and sizing its shell; now working out broken shell fragments scattered around the rim with varying angles and heights.

Working out the rotation math so each shard tilts to point radially outward from the egg's center...

Now I'm placing the loose shell pieces scattered on the ground near the egg, giving each an irregular outline and slight thickness and curl to look like broken fragments.

I thought about adding a small shell cap on the dragon's head but decided to skip that detail. For the egg interior, I'm adding a soft yolk-colored disc at the bottom of the shell to suggest the gooey contents inside.

Now I'm planning the paint spots on the eggshell using a cream base with brownish freckles, and starting to sketch out the body sweep geometry -- using a curved spine path with a slight belly bulge, followed by a tapering neck sweep.

Adjusting the body radius function so it smoothly tapers down to match the neck's starting radius, avoiding a visible seam where the two sweeps join...

Adding smoke puffs, teeth positions, and jaw geometry...

Still placing anatomy pieces...

Still working out the spade geometry...

Finishing toes with low-poly sphere eyes for a simpler look, then wrapping up the metadata and finalizing the write.
